title: Rescuing an untested project: 15 tests and 3 bugs that had been hiding for months
pitch: You take an expense tracker under a hundred lines long, that works "more or less" and doesn't have a single test, and in one afternoon you leave it with 15 automated tests that run in under a second and three real bugs fixed. You do it with an AI assistant, but on a separate branch and reviewing the diff line by line before merging: exactly how it's done at a company.
outcome: A GitHub repository with a clean history, a CLAUDE.md that any assistant reads on arrival, 15 passing tests, 100% coverage on the logic file, and a green check in the Actions tab every time you push code. Plus a three-minute story to tell in an interview: what bug each test was hiding and how you found it.
requires: Python 3.11 or higher installed. Check with python --version in the terminal: it has to answer with a number, not an error.
Git installed (git --version). On Windows it also installs Git Bash, the command window we'll use throughout the project.
A text editor for coding: VS Code works and is free.

A code assistant with access to the folder: Claude Code (included in the Claude Pro plan, about $20/month), GitHub Copilot (has a free plan with 2,000 completions and 50 chat messages a month), or Cursor (limited free plan). If you go with pay-as-you-go API, this whole project costs $2-4.
A GitHub account, free, for the last step. Without it you can still do the first eight steps.
No need to know how to program. You'll be reading Python code and understanding what it does, which isn't the same as writing it from scratch.

structure.what: All the program logic: saving, summing, filtering by date, searching, and calculating VAT. It's the only file that gets tested, and where the three bugs live.
What you run from the terminal. It only reads what you type and prints it to screen; it makes no decisions. That's why it doesn't need testing.
The 15 tests. Each one calls a function in gastos.py with specific data and checks the result is what it should be.
The file your assistant reads when it opens the folder. It contains the project's commands and rules: where tests go, not to touch the real data file, not to invent dependencies.
Four lines of configuration that tell pytest where the tests are and where the code is. Without this, the tests can't find gastos.py.
The list of tools the project needs. It lets another computer (or GitHub) install exactly the same thing with a single command.
What Git should never save: the virtual environment, temp files, your real expenses, and any file with keys.
Instructions for GitHub to run the 15 tests alone, on a clean machine, every time you push code.

steps.title: Set up the ground: folder, Git, virtual environment, and pytest
steps.why: Before testing anything you need somewhere to put it. Here you set up four pieces: a folder, a Git repository so you can go back if something breaks, a virtual environment so you don't clutter your computer with loose libraries, and pytest, the program that runs the tests. You create the .gitignore right away, before the first commit: if your data gets into the history once, getting it out later is a mess.
steps.code:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Open Git Bash (on Windows it comes with Git: right-click on the
# desktop > "Open Git Bash here"). On Mac or Linux, the Terminal.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Project folder and Git repository.
#    A repository is the version history: every time you save
#    progress, Git keeps a snapshot you can return to.
mkdir gastos-cli
cd gastos-cli
git init -b main

# 2. Virtual environment: an isolated copy of Python, just for this
#    project. Anything you install inside it doesn't clutter your computer.
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/Scripts/activate    # Windows (Git Bash)
# source .venv/bin/activate      # macOS and Linux: use this one and delete the one above

# 3. The project's two tools.
#    pytest runs the tests. pytest-cov measures how much code they touch.
#    Both free, about 3 MB to download.
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install pytest pytest-cov

# 4. Tests folder and config files.
mkdir tests

cat > requirements.txt <<'FIN'
pytest>=8.0
pytest-cov>=5.0
FIN

cat > pytest.ini <<'FIN'
[pytest]
pythonpath = .
testpaths = tests
FIN

# .gitignore = the list of things Git must NEVER save.
# This is where your real data and any file with keys go.
cat > .gitignore <<'FIN'
.venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.pytest_cache/
.coverage
htmlcov/
gastos.json
.env
FIN

# 5. First snapshot of the project.
git add .
git commit -m "Startup: pytest configuration"

pytest --version
git log --oneline
steps.expected: pytest --version answers with something like "pytest 8.3.5". git log --oneline shows a single line with a seven-character code and the text "Startup: pytest configuration". At the start of the terminal line, (.venv) will have appeared: that means the virtual environment is active.
steps.trouble: On Windows, if typing python opens the Microsoft Store or nothing happens: Windows has a fake shortcut in place there. Use py instead of python (py --version, py -m venv .venv) or reinstall Python from python.org, checking the "Add python.exe to PATH" box. The other typical error is at commit time: "Please tell me who you are." It means Git doesn't know your name. Run git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@email.com" and repeat the commit.

steps.title: Bring in the legacy code, the code with not a single test
steps.why: This is the real starting point of almost any job: a program someone wrote, that's in use, and that nobody knows for sure fully works. Save it exactly as is, without changing a comma, even if something looks off. What matters right now is having the problem in front of you, not fixing it. Notice one thing: the data file's path comes from an environment variable, it's not hard-coded. That's what will later let the tests write to a throwaway file.
steps.expected: A gastos.py file of about 80 lines inside gastos-cli. Run python -c "import gastos; print(gastos.con_iva(100))" from the project folder: it has to print 121.0. If it prints that, Python understands the file and there are no copy-paste typos.
steps.trouble: "IndentationError: unexpected indent" or "unindent does not match": extra spaces snuck into the start of some line while pasting. In Python, indentation isn't decoration, it marks what's nested inside what. Delete the file, copy the whole block again in one go, and paste it into an empty file, without typing anything beforehand.

steps.title: Run it and check that it "works"
steps.why: Before touching anything you need to see the program alive. You'll log three March expenses and ask for the month's total. Everything will look correct. The interesting part comes after: two of those numbers that now look normal to you are wrong, and there's no way to tell just by looking. That's exactly the whole point of this project.
steps.code:
"""Command-line interface: what you run from the terminal.

Save it as cli.py, next to gastos.py. This file only reads what you
type and prints it nicely. All the logic is in gastos.py, and that's
why gastos.py is what we're going to test.
"""

import argparse
import gastos


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Personal expense manager")
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="orden", required=True)

    # No accents in the command names: typing them in the terminal has
    # to be fast and not fail on any keyboard.
    p_add = sub.add_parser("anadir", help="Log an expense")
    p_add.add_argument("concepto")
    p_add.add_argument("importe", type=float)
    p_add.add_argument("--fecha", default=None, help="YYYY-MM-DD")

    sub.add_parser("listar", help="Show all expenses")

    p_total = sub.add_parser("total", help="Sum a date range")
    p_total.add_argument("desde")
    p_total.add_argument("hasta")

    sub.add_parser("media", help="Average spend per day")

    p_buscar = sub.add_parser("buscar", help="Search by description")
    p_buscar.add_argument("texto")

    args = parser.parse_args()
    datos = gastos.cargar()

    if args.orden == "anadir":
        g = gastos.anadir(args.concepto, args.importe, args.fecha)
        print("Saved: {} {:.2f} EUR ({})".format(
            g["concepto"], g["importe"], g["fecha"]))

    elif args.orden == "listar":
        if not datos:
            print("No expenses yet.")
        for g in datos:
            print("{}  {:>8.2f} EUR  {}".format(
                g["fecha"], g["importe"], g["concepto"]))

    elif args.orden == "total":
        sel = gastos.entre_fechas(datos, args.desde, args.hasta)
        print("{} expenses between {} and {}: {:.2f} EUR".format(
            len(sel), args.desde, args.hasta, gastos.total(sel)))

    elif args.orden == "media":
        print("Average per day: {:.2f} EUR".format(gastos.media_diaria(datos)))

    elif args.orden == "buscar":
        encontrados = gastos.buscar(datos, args.texto)
        print("{} results".format(len(encontrados)))
        for g in encontrados:
            print("{}  {:>8.2f} EUR  {}".format(
                g["fecha"], g["importe"], g["concepto"]))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()


# Once saved, try it from the terminal (one line at a time):
#
#   python cli.py anadir "Mercadona" 42.10 --fecha 2026-03-01
#   python cli.py anadir "Gasolina Repsol" 60 --fecha 2026-03-15
#   python cli.py anadir "mercadona online" 18.90 --fecha 2026-03-31
#   python cli.py listar
#   python cli.py total 2026-03-01 2026-03-31
#   python cli.py media
#   python cli.py buscar Mercadona
#
# And save the project exactly as it was, untested:
#
#   git add gastos.py cli.py
#   git commit -m "Legacy project, as I received it"
steps.expected: python cli.py listar prints the three lines sorted by date with their amounts. python cli.py media answers "Average per day: 40.33 EUR". python cli.py total 2026-03-01 2026-03-31 answers "2 expenses between 2026-03-01 and 2026-03-31: 102.10 EUR". Write that number down; we'll come back to it. And python cli.py buscar Mercadona says "1 results".
steps.trouble: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gastos'": you're running cli.py from a different folder. Type pwd in the terminal; it has to end in /gastos-cli. If not, run cd gastos-cli. If the error is "invalid choice: 'anadir'", you typed the command with an accented character: in the terminal it's typed anadir, no accent.

steps.title: Write CLAUDE.md, the contract with your assistant
steps.why: An assistant reads your code, but the code doesn't say how you work here. It doesn't say tests go in tests/, or that you don't want new dependencies, or that no test can write to your real expenses. Without that file you end up repeating the same four sentences in every conversation, and every session still invents different conventions. With it, the rules are written once and hold for every session, every assistant, and anyone who opens the project. Rule 6 is the most important of all: it forbids fixing anything while writing tests. If you let it do both at once, it'll write tests that pass against code it just changed itself, and you won't have tested anything.
steps.code:
# CLAUDE.md is the file your assistant reads when it enters the folder.
# It's its contract: what can't be inferred just by reading the code.
# Create it at the project root (next to gastos.py).

cat > CLAUDE.md <<'FIN'
# gastos-cli

Command-line program for logging personal expenses.
Python 3.11 or higher, no dependencies beyond pytest.

## Project commands

- Run the program: `python cli.py listar`
- Run the tests: `pytest -v`
- See coverage: `pytest --cov=gastos --cov-report=term-missing`

## What's in each file

- `gastos.py` — all the logic. It's the only thing that's tested.
- `cli.py` — only reads arguments and prints. No logic goes here.
- `tests/test_gastos.py` — the tests.

## Rules when working here

1. Tests go in `tests/`, with pytest. No unittest, and no new
   dependency without asking me first.
2. No test may write to the real `gastos.json`. Use
   `tmp_path` and `monkeypatch.setenv("GASTOS_FICHERO", ...)`.
3. Descriptive test names in Spanish:
   `test_entre_fechas_incluye_el_ultimo_dia`, never `test_1`.
4. No API keys, tokens, or real emails in the code or in
   this file. Anything secret comes from environment variables, and `.env`
   is in `.gitignore`.
5. One change, one branch. Never work directly on `main`.
6. If you find a bug while writing tests, don't fix it at the
   same time: write the test that proves it, leave it red, and tell me.

## Data

The `GASTOS_FICHERO` environment variable points to the data JSON.
If it isn't set, `gastos.json` in the current folder is used.
FIN

git add CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Add CLAUDE.md with the project rules"
steps.expected: A CLAUDE.md file at the project root and a second commit in git log --oneline. Open it in the editor and read it: it should fit in a page and a half. If it grows bigger, nobody reads it, not your assistant and not you.
steps.trouble: If you use PowerShell instead of Git Bash, the cat > file <<'FIN' block doesn't work and just hangs waiting. Press Ctrl+C, open Git Bash (right-click the folder > Open Git Bash here), and try again. An alternative that works anywhere: create the CLAUDE.md file by hand in VS Code and paste in just the text between FIN and FIN.

steps.title: Open a branch and ask the assistant for the tests
steps.why: Never work directly on main. A branch is a parallel copy: you do whatever you want inside it and main stays untouched until you decide to merge. If the assistant makes a mess, you delete the branch and nothing happened. And the request matters as much as the branch: don't tell it "write tests", tell it what cases you want, with what tool, what it can't touch, and to give you the full output even if it fails. The instruction not to fix anything is the key: you want to see the original code fail.
steps.code:
# A branch is a parallel line of work. What you do inside it doesn't
# touch main until you merge it yourself. If it goes wrong, delete it
# and nothing happened.
git switch -c pruebas
git branch          # shows you both branches, with * on the current one

# Now open your assistant IN THIS FOLDER and paste it the request below.
# Everything starting with # is a comment: if you paste them into the
# terminal they do nothing, so you can copy the whole block without worry.
#
# ------------------- REQUEST FOR THE ASSISTANT -------------------
# Read CLAUDE.md before writing a single line.
#
# Write the tests for gastos.py in tests/test_gastos.py.
#
# Conditions:
# - pytest only. No new dependencies.
# - Do NOT touch gastos.py yet, even if you spot bugs. If you find one,
#   write the test that proves it, leave it red, and tell me at the end.
# - No test may write to my real gastos.json. Make a
#   fixture called fichero_temporal with tmp_path and
#   monkeypatch.setenv("GASTOS_FICHERO", ...).
# - Cases I want covered: loading with no file; anadir (saves to
#   disk, two expenses in a row, strips spaces from the description, rejects 0, and
#   rejects negatives); total (normal and empty list); entre_fechas
#   including the last day; media_diaria (three days and an empty list);
#   buscar case-insensitively; con_iva at 21% and 10%.
# - Names in Spanish, one per behavior.
#
# When you're done, run pytest -v and paste me the full output,
# including whatever fails. Don't fix anything.
# ---------------------- END OF REQUEST ------------------------
steps.expected: git branch shows two lines, main and pruebas, with an asterisk in front of pruebas. And the assistant hands back a tests/test_gastos.py file along with a pytest output where things are red. If it comes back all green, be suspicious: either it fixed the code on its own (check git status and git diff gastos.py) or it wrote tests that don't check anything.
steps.trouble: "git: 'switch' is not a git command": you have a Git version from before 2019. Use git checkout -b pruebas, which does the same thing. And if the assistant says it can't find the files, you've opened it in the wrong folder: close it and reopen it inside gastos-cli.

steps.title: Run the tests and look at the three red ones
steps.why: This is the moment of the project. Fifteen tests, three red, and the three red ones are real bugs that had been sitting there for months: the date filter was eating the last day of the month (that's why March's total came out 102.10 instead of 121.00), the average crashed the program when there were no expenses at all, and the search was case-sensitive, so searching "mercadona" didn't find "Mercadona". None of the three shows up from skimming the code. Read the tests before running them: they're fifteen five-line paragraphs, and each one's name says what behavior it defends.
steps.code:
"""Tests for gastos.py.

This is what should have come out. Compare it with what the assistant
wrote you: keep the best of each and paste the result into
tests/test_gastos.py.

Run with:  pytest -v
"""

import json
import pytest
import gastos


@pytest.fixture
def fichero_temporal(tmp_path, monkeypatch):
    """Each test writes to a new file that gets deleted afterward.

    A fixture is a setup pytest builds before the test. tmp_path is a
    temporary folder; monkeypatch changes the environment variable only
    during the test. Result: your real expenses are never touched.
    """
    ruta = tmp_path / "gastos.json"
    monkeypatch.setenv("GASTOS_FICHERO", str(ruta))
    return ruta


# Fixed data for tests that don't write to disk.
# Three March expenses, on three different days: 42.10 + 60.00 + 18.90 = 121.00
MARZO = [
    {"concepto": "Mercadona", "importe": 42.10, "fecha": "2026-03-01"},
    {"concepto": "Gasolina Repsol", "importe": 60.00, "fecha": "2026-03-15"},
    {"concepto": "mercadona online", "importe": 18.90, "fecha": "2026-03-31"},
]


def test_cargar_sin_fichero_devuelve_lista_vacia(fichero_temporal):
    assert gastos.cargar() == []


def test_anadir_guarda_en_disco(fichero_temporal):
    gastos.anadir("Cafe", 1.60, "2026-03-02")
    guardados = json.loads(fichero_temporal.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    assert len(guardados) == 1
    assert guardados[0]["concepto"] == "Cafe"
    assert guardados[0]["importe"] == 1.6


def test_anadir_dos_veces_conserva_el_primero(fichero_temporal):
    gastos.anadir("Cafe", 1.60, "2026-03-02")
    gastos.anadir("Pan", 2.40, "2026-03-02")
    assert len(gastos.cargar()) == 2


def test_anadir_quita_espacios_del_concepto(fichero_temporal):
    gasto = gastos.anadir("   Farmacia  ", 12.0, "2026-03-03")
    assert gasto["concepto"] == "Farmacia"


def test_anadir_rechaza_importe_cero(fichero_temporal):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        gastos.anadir("Nada", 0, "2026-03-04")


def test_anadir_rechaza_importe_negativo(fichero_temporal):
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        gastos.anadir("Devolucion", -5, "2026-03-04")


def test_total_suma_los_importes():
    assert gastos.total(MARZO) == 121.00


def test_total_de_lista_vacia_es_cero():
    assert gastos.total([]) == 0


def test_entre_fechas_incluye_el_ultimo_dia():
    # From March 1st to 31st all three expenses fall in, the 31st one too.
    seleccion = gastos.entre_fechas(MARZO, "2026-03-01", "2026-03-31")
    assert len(seleccion) == 3


def test_entre_fechas_deja_fuera_lo_que_no_toca():
    seleccion = gastos.entre_fechas(MARZO, "2026-03-02", "2026-03-20")
    assert [g["concepto"] for g in seleccion] == ["Gasolina Repsol"]


def test_media_diaria_de_tres_dias():
    # 121.00 across 3 distinct days = 40.33
    assert gastos.media_diaria(MARZO) == pytest.approx(40.33, abs=0.01)


def test_media_diaria_de_lista_vacia_es_cero():
    assert gastos.media_diaria([]) == 0


def test_buscar_ignora_mayusculas():
    # "MERCADONA" has to find both "Mercadona" and "mercadona online".
    assert len(gastos.buscar(MARZO, "MERCADONA")) == 2


def test_con_iva_del_21_por_ciento():
    assert gastos.con_iva(100) == 121.00


def test_con_iva_reducido_del_10():
    assert gastos.con_iva(50, tipo=10) == 55.00
steps.expected: pytest -v ends with the line "3 failed, 12 passed in 0.1s" in red. Right above it you'll see the three culprits: test_entre_fechas_incluye_el_ultimo_dia (assert 2 == 3), test_media_diaria_de_lista_vacia_es_cero (ZeroDivisionError: division by zero), and test_buscar_ignora_mayusculas (assert 0 == 2). If that's exactly what you get, you're right on track: the red ones are the goal, not a problem.
steps.trouble: "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gastos'" when running pytest: the pytest.ini file with the pythonpath = . line is missing, or you saved it in the wrong folder. It has to be next to gastos.py, not inside tests/. If you get "fixture 'fichero_temporal' not found", you pasted the tests without the function above marked with @pytest.fixture: copy the whole file again.

steps.title: Fix the three bugs and check the coverage
steps.why: Now, and only now, do you touch the code: with fifteen tests set up that will warn you the moment you break anything else. It's three tiny changes, one symbol and two lines, and that's exactly the kind of bug that survives for years in an untested project. When you're done, measure the coverage, which is the percentage of code lines the tests actually exercise. Watch out for confusing it: high coverage doesn't mean correct code, it means there's no code left unexamined. Those are different things.
steps.expected: pytest -v ends in green with "15 passed in 0.1s". And pytest --cov=gastos --cov-report=term-missing prints a table with gastos.py, 36 statements, 0 missing, and 100% in the Cover column. Run python cli.py total 2026-03-01 2026-03-31 again: now it says 3 expenses and 121.00 EUR, not 102.10. That's the bug you'd been chasing for two hours, now fixed.
steps.trouble: If test_buscar_ignora_mayusculas still fails, you only changed one of the two parts: you need texto = texto.lower() at the top AND .lower() on g["concepto"] too. If you compare only one side, it still finds nothing. And if "unrecognized arguments: --cov" shows up, pytest-cov wasn't installed: pip install pytest-cov with the virtual environment active.

steps.title: Review the diff, make two commits, and merge into main
steps.why: The diff is the one thing standing between you and blindly trusting a machine. It's the line-by-line differences between what was there and what's there now: you read it in full, and if something you didn't ask for shows up, you take it out. It's the single most valuable habit in this whole area, because assistants don't usually break things loudly, they break them sideways: renaming a function, changing a default value, deleting a comment that explained why something was that way. Afterward you merge the branch into main, which is the operation that makes the work official.
steps.code:
# 1. What's currently changed.
git status

# 2. The diff: the differences, line by line. Lines starting with -
#    are going away, lines starting with + are coming in. READ IT ALL
#    before saving anything. It's the step that separates using an
#    assistant from trusting it blindly. Leave the viewer with q.
git diff gastos.py

# You should have three changes and only three: <= in entre_fechas, the
# if in media_diaria, and the two .lower() in buscar. If you see anything
# else (a renamed function, a new import, a deleted comment),
# that's exactly the kind of thing an assistant slips in when no one's watching.

# 3. Two separate commits, even though you did it all in one go. Git
#    lets you choose which files go into each snapshot, and a history
#    that reads well is what saves you six months from now.
git add tests/test_gastos.py
git commit -m "Tests for gastos.py: 15 cases with pytest"

git add gastos.py
git commit -m "Fix the range's last day, the average with an empty list, and case-sensitive search"

# 4. What this branch does to main, in summary.
git diff main..pruebas --stat

# 5. Merge. First, check how main looks: untested.
git switch main
pytest -v            # "no tests ran": there are none in main yet

git merge pruebas
pytest -v            # now yes: 15 passed

git log --oneline --graph --all

# WARNING: if the assistant ever suggests "git reset --hard",
# "git checkout -- file", or "git push --force", stop. Those three
# delete work with no trash can and no undo. Ask first.

# 6. Push it to GitHub. First create the empty repository on github.com
#    (New button, no README, no .gitignore), then, replacing YOUR-USERNAME:
#
#    git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/gastos-cli.git
#    git push -u origin main
#
# WARNING: if you make it public, everything you push stays public
# forever, even if you delete it afterward. Check first that gastos.json and
# .env are still in .gitignore and don't show up in "git status".
steps.expected: git diff gastos.py shows you exactly three blocks with red and green lines. The two commits show up in git log --oneline --graph --all, which draws the history with lines and asterisks. After the merge, pytest -v gives 15 passed while on main. Before the merge, on main, pytest says "no tests ran": that's the snapshot of how the project was when you inherited it.
steps.trouble: If git diff opens a screen that won't close with anything, you're in Git's pager: press q. If merging shows "CONFLICT", main changed underneath you (unusual if you're working alone): type git merge --abort to reset everything and try again. And if git push answers "repository not found", you haven't created the repository on github.com yet, or you typed your username wrong in the URL.

steps.title: Make the tests run on their own on every push
steps.why: A test that only runs when you remember isn't much use. With this file, GitHub spins up a clean Linux machine on every push, installs Python, installs the dependencies, and runs your fifteen tests. If anything breaks, you get an email and a red X shows up next to the commit. It's free and unlimited on public repositories; on private ones you get 2,000 free minutes a month, and this takes about 40 seconds per push, so you won't come close. When you save it: git add .github, then git commit -m "Automated tests on every push" and git push.
steps.code:
# Save this at .github/workflows/pruebas.yml
# (yes, the folder starts with a dot, and there are two nested folders).
# Indentation matters: in YAML, two extra spaces change the
# meaning. Copy and paste as-is.

name: pruebas

# When it runs: on every push to any branch and on every pull request.
on:
  push:
    branches: ["**"]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  pytest:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest    # GitHub spins up a clean Linux machine
    steps:
      - name: Check out the code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: |
          python -m pip install --upgrade pip
          pip install -r requirements.txt

      - name: Run the tests
        run: pytest -v --cov=gastos --cov-report=term-missing
steps.expected: A minute after pushing, in your repository's Actions tab a run called "pruebas" shows up with a spinning yellow circle. Forty seconds later a green check appears. Click into it, and in the "Run the tests" step you'll see the same pytest output you see on your computer: 15 passed and the coverage table at 100%.
steps.trouble: "Invalid workflow file": the YAML indentation got scrambled while pasting, almost always in the run block with the pipe symbol. GitHub tells you the exact line. If nothing shows up in Actions, check the path: it has to be .github/workflows/pruebas.yml, with the dot before github and workflows in plural. One character wrong and GitHub doesn't even know it exists.

checks: pytest -v ends with "15 passed" and takes under a second. If it takes more than five, some test is touching disk or network where it shouldn't.
Delete gastos.json from the folder, run pytest, and check it still doesn't exist. No test can create or modify your real data: that's what the GASTOS_FICHERO environment variable is for.
pytest --cov=gastos --cov-report=term-missing gives 100% and the Missing column is empty.
git log --oneline shows at least five commits with messages that make sense without opening the code, and git branch shows main and pruebas.
You can explain the three bugs from memory: what each was, which test caught it, and which line fixed it. If you can't, you haven't read the diff.
Break the code on purpose: remove a .lower() from buscar and run pytest. It has to turn red in under a second. If it stays green, that test isn't protecting anything.
In GitHub's Actions tab there's a green check on the latest commit.
extend: Easy, five minutes: enforce a minimum coverage. Change the workflow's last line to pytest --cov=gastos --cov-fail-under=90. From then on, if someone adds a function without testing it, GitHub puts up the red X and everyone finds out.

Medium, half an hour: group the VAT cases with @pytest.mark.parametrize. A single test function with the table (0, 100), (4, 104), (10, 110), (21, 121) replaces four nearly identical functions. When a tax rate changes, you touch one line instead of four. Ask the assistant to write it and compare its version with the four you had.

Harder, an afternoon: set up a hook that stops you before pushing anything broken. Create .git/hooks/pre-commit with two lines (#!/bin/sh and pytest -q || exit 1) and make it executable with chmod +x. From that moment Git rejects any commit with red tests, on your machine, before anyone else sees it. One warning: that folder doesn't travel with the repository, so each team member has to set it up themselves. To actually share it, use the pre-commit tool, which does get versioned.
defend: "Did you write those tests, or did the AI write them for you?" — The assistant drafted them and I reviewed them one by one before accepting them. I contributed the three things that matter: the CLAUDE.md with the rules (pytest only, no test touches the real data file, don't fix while writing tests), the specific list of behaviors I wanted covered, and the diff review before merging. I threw out two tests that weren't testing anything, one that just checked a list was a list. The fact that a machine typed it doesn't change who's on the hook if this breaks on Monday.

"What's the point of a CLAUDE.md if the assistant can already read the code?" — The code says what the program does; it doesn't say how we work here. That file holds what can't be inferred from reading: that tests go in tests/ and run with pytest -v, that no new dependencies get added, that no test may write to the real gastos.json, and that if it finds a bug it writes the test and doesn't fix it. Without that you repeat the same four sentences every conversation and every session invents new conventions. It's context written once that serves every session and whoever opens the project tomorrow.

"The fifteen tests are green. How do you know they're actually worth anything?" — Because I saw them red first. That's the whole point: when I wrote them against the legacy code, three out of fifteen failed, and all three were real bugs already affecting the user. The date filter was eating the last day of the month, so March's total came out €102.10 instead of €121.00. The average divided by zero and crashed on the very first day of use. And the search was case-sensitive. A test that has never been red doesn't prove anything, it just gives false peace of mind. If you want to check it right now, I'll remove a .lower() from the buscar function and you'll have it red in two seconds.
